claims.text: Incorporating nanoscale oxide dispersoids into refractory high-entropy alloys will improve mechanical performance under high-temperature conditions.
Incorporating nanoscale oxide dispersoids into refractory high-entropy alloys will improve mechanical performance under irradiation.
The oxide-dispersoid intervention will not compromise thermal stability.
The oxide-dispersoid intervention will not compromise irradiation stability.
Controlled oxygen addition or ex situ oxide introduction during processing can produce a nanoscale oxide dispersion in the alloy.
The intervention will create a stable dispersion of nanoscale oxide particles within the refractory high-entropy-alloy matrix.
Oxide dispersoids pin grain boundaries and restrict grain-boundary movement.
Oxide dispersoids serve as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Defect-sink behavior mitigates the accumulation of irradiation-induced defects.
Relative to an otherwise identical alloy without dispersoids, the oxide-containing alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to an otherwise identical alloy without dispersoids, the oxide-containing alloy will have improved creep resistance.
Relative to an otherwise identical alloy without dispersoids, the oxide-containing alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced swelling.
The beneficial effects depend on the oxide dispersoids remaining uniformly dispersed.
An excessive oxide volume fraction or oxide agglomeration may cause brittleness.
An excessive oxide volume fraction or oxide agglomeration may cause phase instability.
The optimal processing parameters and oxide volume fraction for obtaining a stable dispersion without adverse effects are not yet precisely determined.
